questions.text: Explain the role of carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, and minerals in the body, with one food source for each.
questions.answer: Carbohydrates give quick energy; rice or roti are major sources. Proteins build and repair the body; dal, eggs and milk are sources. Fats give long-lasting energy and store warmth; ghee, butter, nuts are sources. Vitamins protect against deficiency diseases and keep tissues healthy; fruits and vegetables are good sources. Minerals like calcium build bones and iron makes blood; milk gives calcium, spinach gives iron. A diet missing any of these can lead to weakness or specific deficiency diseases.
questions.explanation: Tests broad understanding of food groups and their roles.

questions.text: A 12-year-old student often complains of weakness and tiredness. Suggest possible nutritional reasons and a plan to improve her diet.
questions.answer: Possible reasons: not enough iron (causing anaemia), not enough proteins, skipping breakfast, eating too many sugary snacks, or not drinking enough water. Plan: (1) Start the day with a real breakfast — poha or paratha plus a glass of milk and a fruit. (2) Lunch: roti, dal, a vegetable like spinach or methi (rich in iron), curd, salad. Add a slice of lemon (vitamin C) to boost iron absorption. (3) Snack: roasted chana or a banana with a glass of milk, instead of biscuits. (4) Dinner: rice or roti, dal, sabzi, and a small bowl of curd. (5) Drink at least 6-8 glasses of water through the day. After 4 weeks, check whether the tiredness has reduced; if not, consult a doctor.
questions.explanation: Tests applying knowledge of nutrition + deficiency symptoms.

questions.text: 'Junk food is not always harmful — it depends on how often you eat it.' Discuss this statement, listing arguments for and against.
questions.answer: For the statement: occasional treats can be part of normal life and don't cause harm if the rest of the diet is balanced. Special foods on festivals or birthdays are part of culture and joy. Eating sweets once in a while doesn't ruin a healthy diet. Against the statement: junk foods are often very high in fat, sugar, and salt, and low in protein, vitamins, and fibre. Eating them too often can lead to weight gain, tooth decay, weak immunity, and even long-term illnesses like diabetes and heart trouble. They also tend to replace better foods. Balanced view: the key is moderation. Eating junk food once in a while is acceptable; making it a regular habit is harmful. The amount, the frequency, and what else is eaten all matter.
questions.explanation: Open-ended; full credit for balanced reasoning.
